adds.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's national 'LGBT rights in Turkey' page is the framework every Turkish province, Isparta included, stands under: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the military: the armed forces' health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual' illness making members unfit for service, and conscripts who declare their homosexuality have to provide photographic proof. Same-sex marriage is not recognised; a 2012 constitutional-writing request to include it was rejected by both the AKP and the MHP. Authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years and police have used tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans; on 14 June 2019 the 7th Izmir Pride, the 3rd Antalya Pride and the 27th Istanbul Pride were banned by the cities' governors. The page also records a February 2026 newspaper report that the government was considering a law criminalising publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex', with a sentence of one to three years in prison.

adds.title: Türkiye - Amnesty International country report (Report 2025/26)
adds.summary: Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) is the enforcement framework a trans visitor stands under in any province, Isparta included: in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained; although in November a court overturned a ban in Istanbul governorate as 'disproportionate' and 'unlawful', prosecutions involving 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an Izmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had engaged in activities outside its stated purpose and shared 'obscene' images incompatible with the law. Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 - an unprecedented assault that would criminalise any expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible - but they were ultimately not submitted to parliament.
